titre: Beta-Carotene Pills Worsened the Cancer They Were Meant to Prevent
accroche: In the mid-1990s, two trials on smokers find the opposite of what they were looking for: one had to be stopped before its planned end.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the 1970s, several observational studies note that people who eat a lot of fruit and vegetables rich in beta-carotene develop fewer lung cancers than others. The hypothesis seems straightforward: this antioxidant, which the body converts into vitamin A, would neutralize the damage caused by tobacco smoke. What remains is to check whether the molecule, isolated from its dietary context and given at high doses, produces the same effect.

## Two independent trials, one signal

The ATBC trial (Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta-Carotene) recruits 29,133 Finnish smokers aged 50 to 69, split between beta-carotene alone, vitamin E alone, both, or a placebo. Published in 1994 in the New England Journal of Medicine after five to eight years of follow-up, the results reverse the starting hypothesis: lung cancer increases by 18% in the beta-carotene group, and total mortality by 8%, driven mainly by deaths from lung cancer and ischemic heart disease.

Two years later, the American CARET trial, run independently of the first on 18,314 smokers, former smokers, and asbestos-exposed workers, finds the same signal: a relative risk of 1.36 for lung cancer incidence and 1.59 for death from that cancer in the treated group. The safety monitoring board stops the trial twenty-one months ahead of schedule, judging that continuing was useless and potentially dangerous.

## What two converging trials shift

Two randomized trials, run on two continents, with different populations and protocols, find the same effect in the same direction: the convergence rules out an isolated statistical fluke in either trial.

What this result shifts is the idea that what is good as a food stays good once concentrated into a pill. The beta-carotene in carrots or spinach comes, in food, together with hundreds of other compounds, at modest and variable doses depending on the meal. Isolated and given continuously at a high dose, in smokers whose lungs are already under chronic oxidative stress, it instead seems to favor the proliferation of already damaged cells. The most discussed hypothesis is that at high concentration, the molecule stops behaving as an antioxidant and ends up producing the opposite effect.

Neither trial says that fruit and vegetables hold no value for lung health. They say that the association observed at the table does not carry over as is into a capsule, a distinction that nutrition research keeps rediscovering for other nutrients.

repere.texte: In the ATBC trial, lung cancer increased by 18% among smokers given beta-carotene compared with placebo, and total mortality by 8%.

carte.punch: The pill meant to protect smokers made worse the very thing it was meant to prevent.
carte.idee: Two independent randomized trials, one Finnish (ATBC, 1994), the other American (CARET, 1996), tested beta-carotene pills in smokers against lung cancer. Both found the opposite: CARET was stopped 21 months early, ATBC found it at its full planned end.

quiz.question: What did the ATBC and CARET trials find in common about beta-carotene pills in smokers?
choix: That beta-carotene pills increased lung cancer in smokers, instead of reducing it
That too many participants refused to keep taking the pills
That beta-carotene caused digestive problems too often to continue
That both trials ran out of funding to continue follow-up
quiz.explication: Both trials found the opposite of what they were testing: beta-carotene pills increased lung cancer incidence and mortality in smokers. CARET was even stopped 21 months early for exactly this reason; ATBC, for its part, ran its follow-up to its planned end and found the same signal. The other three statements contradict the two studies cited in the entry.
